questions.q: Why is GPU capacity planning a genuinely different problem from capacity planning for general-purpose CPU compute?
options: GPUs never need quota increases of any kind
A specific high-demand GPU SKU in a specific region is physically constrained, so a scale-up request can fail outright as an allocation failure rather than just being slow
GPUs autoscale instantly in every cloud region with no limits
CPU instances are actually scarcer than GPU instances in most regions
questions.explain: Unlike general-purpose compute, where headroom is usually abundant, a popular GPU SKU can simply be unavailable in a region when demand is high, independent of budget.

questions.q: What does a cloud provider's GPU quota actually limit?
options: The number of software licenses installed on a VM
The price charged per GPU-hour
How many instances of a given GPU family your subscription/account can provision in a region by default, regardless of whether physical hardware exists
The maximum number of regions a subscription can use
questions.explain: Quota is an account-level ceiling the provider sets independent of physical data-center capacity; raising it is a request, not a guarantee that hardware is available.

questions.q: What do Azure On-Demand Capacity Reservations and AWS Capacity Blocks for ML both let you do?
options: Pre-book specific GPU capacity for a defined window, trading flexibility and standing cost for a guarantee of availability
Avoid ever needing a quota increase
Automatically migrate a training job to a cheaper CPU instance
Bypass regional data residency requirements
questions.explain: Both are reservation mechanisms: you pay for held capacity (standing, or for a specific future window) in exchange for the provider guaranteeing it's there when you need it.

questions.q: What role does a 'fallback hierarchy' play in GPU capacity planning?
options: It eliminates the need to ever forecast GPU demand
It guarantees the lowest possible price for every workload
It replaces the need for quota requests entirely
It defines a planned sequence of next-best options — an alternate SKU, an alternate region, or a degraded mode — so a shortfall degrades the workload instead of failing it outright
questions.explain: A fallback hierarchy turns an unavailable preferred SKU into a planned, documented degradation path rather than an unhandled failure.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when does reserving GPU capacity ahead of time make the most sense?
options: Only for workloads that run entirely on CPUs
For predictable, large-scale demand that can be forecast ahead of time, such as a quarter's training roadmap or an already-committed launch date
Never — on-demand capacity is always sufficient for GPUs
For every single GPU need a business has, with no exceptions
questions.explain: Reservations trade flexibility and standing cost for guaranteed availability, which pays off for forecastable, high-stakes demand rather than every incidental GPU need.
